name: getInstalledRelatedApps
plain: Lets a site check whether its own native app is installed.
meaning: Reveals only whether the site's declared related app is installed, to hide install banners.

access.iframe: Same as top level; cross-origin iframes need a permissions policy where listed

chrome.note: Supported on Windows for checking of Universal Windows Platform (UWP) app installation. Resolves with an empty array on other platforms.

edge.note: Supported on Windows for checking of Universal Windows Platform (UWP) app installation. Resolves with an empty array on other platforms.

chrome_android.note: Supports checking of Progressive Web App (PWA) installation.

samsung.note: Supports checking of Progressive Web App (PWA) installation.

data.metric: Lets a site check whether its own native app is installed.

fields.name: platform
fields.range: play, chromeos_play, webapp, windows, f-droid, amazon

limits.headline: Can check if its own app is installed, but not see your other apps
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads, to show Open in app or Get the app.
can: Check if its own app is installed on your device
Show Open in app instead of Get the app
Check apps that the site has linked to itself in its settings
cannot: See a list of your installed apps
Check apps that are not linked to the site
Work in Firefox, Safari or on iPhone
Say what version or how often you use the app
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge on Android support it. Firefox, Safari and iPhone do not.

story.what_it_is: A site can check if its own app is installed on your device.

marketing.name: getInstalledRelatedApps()
marketing.pitch: Chrome's docs say the API lets a site check whether its own app is installed.

story.for_you: You never see it. A site can hide its 'install our app' banner if it finds the app on your device.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to hide install prompts and to nudge you into the app where they make more money. The result also tells them whether you are an app user, which they can use in profiles.

use_cases.example: A store hides its install banner when you already have the app.
A social site sends you to its app instead of asking you to install.
A music site skips the 'get our app' pop up if it is installed.
A web game page hides its install ad once you installed the app.
An ad system treats app users as a different, more valuable audience.
A product team counts how many web visitors also have the app.

technical_bounds: Only apps listed in manifest related_applications that also link back
